name: Iris Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week is lectures on chemistry and how medicines work in the body, a lab on Wednesdays where I mostly spill things, and choir practice on Thursday nights. I'm studying pharmacy, and my family has run a small pharmacy on the high street in my home town for twenty years, so I'm already the one my friends ask about their pills. I use an AI assistant for almost everything, from planning my study week to quizzing me on drug names. On Saturdays I take the train home and work the counter for my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, we can all stop panicking and get on with it. I'd tell my coursemates it's still useful for study, but not a miracle. I'd post a joke about the assistant misspelling a drug name, which it did last week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit uneasy even then. The pharmacy is small and the chains keep opening cheaper branches, so a plateau doesn't save us from that. It just means the pressure stays the same, which is already quite a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my degree, keep working Saturdays, and ask my mum if I can take over the ordering and stock records. I'd use the assistant to learn faster and would try to bring a simple stock tool into the shop. I'd also join a pharmacy students' society to get contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not that anything dramatic happens, it's that the small things pile up: thin margins, long hours, and a rent rise every few years. I love the shop, but I know what it costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing much changes. What about the family pharmacy still keeps your mum up at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the rent and the chain across the road. When the chain pharmacy opened across the road, our family shop lost a fifth of its regular customers in a year, and a plateau doesn't fix that. I feel it every Saturday I'm on the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you still use your assistant in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, absolutely. It's good for revision, and it's good at explaining interactions between medicines, though I always check it against the textbook. I'm not going to stop using something that works.

say: I'd say we can all **stop panicking**, as AI is useful but no miracle.
I'd post a joke about the assistant **misspelling** a drug name.
think: Privately I'm **uneasy**, because chains keep opening cheaper branches.
A plateau leaves the **pressure** on our small shop unchanged.
do: Ask my mum to let me run **stock records** and ordering.
Bring a simple **stock tool** into the shop and join a pharmacy students' society.
feel: **Uneasy**, because small pressures pile up even when nothing dramatic happens.
S0.quote: When the chain pharmacy opened across the road, our family shop lost a fifth of its regular customers in a year, and a plateau doesn't fix that.
fieldNote: Her **unease** comes from the chain across the road, not from AI.
She volunteers to **run stock records**, a practical, adaptive move.
She is **proud of the shop** and open about its costs.

steps.text: Take over ordering and stock records at the family pharmacy on Saturdays
Try a simple stock-tracking tool at the shop
Keep studying and working Saturdays at the counter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity if we use it well, and that small businesses need access to the same tools as the big chains. I'd tell my coursemates to learn the systems early, since we'll be hired for it. I'd post a thread about what worked for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be steady, with an eye on the shop. Dispensing, stock checks and insurance forms could be done by software, which saves time, but could also mean pharmacies need fewer staff. If chains get it first, we'd be squeezed again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to use pharmacy software and automated dispensing, and ask my mum if we can trial a tool for ordering. I'd start offering things the machine can't do, like medicine reviews and chats with older customers. I'd also look at which services the pharmacy could add, such as vaccinations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy together. I love tech, and I can see the shop running smoother, but I can also see the chains running over us. It's a race I'd like to be in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a pharmacist's day do you think software does first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stock counting, ordering, checking prescriptions for errors, and sending the insurance claims. My mum spends about a day a week on stock counting and insurance claims, and if software takes that, she can talk to customers, which she loves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a small shop like yours cope better or worse than a chain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better in some ways, because we can move faster than a chain's head office. Worse because the chains can pay for the best systems. If prices come down, we win. If they don't, we're in trouble.

say: I'd say it's an **opportunity** if small businesses get the same tools as chains.
I'd tell coursemates to **learn the systems** early.
think: Privately I'm **steady** but watching the shop: fewer staff might be needed.
If chains get the tools first, we'd be **squeezed** again.
do: Learn **pharmacy software** and automated dispensing, and ask my mum to trial an ordering tool.
Offer things a machine can't, like **medicine reviews** and vaccinations.
feel: **Excited and uneasy** together, in a race I'd like to be in.
S1.quote: My mum spends about a day a week on stock counting and insurance claims, and if software takes that, she can talk to customers, which she loves.
fieldNote: She sees **medicine reviews** as the human service a small shop can add.
She frames the shop's future as **a race against chains**.
Her excitement is real, but her **unease** about scale is too.

steps.text: Learn pharmacy dispensing software and ask my mum to trial an ordering tool
Use AI to revise drug interactions and check it against the textbook
Plan medicine reviews and vaccination services for the shop
Take pharmacy-specific modules on clinical services

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules so small shops aren't wiped out before they can adapt. I'd ask the pharmacy association what they plan to do and offer to speak on a student panel. I'd keep my tone practical, not panicky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be anxious and a little angry. The shop is how my family lives, and two years is not enough to change how a pharmacy works. If a chain gets full automation first, we're finished before I even qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home that weekend and sit down with my parents to look at the shop's accounts and see what we can adjust. I'd throw myself into learning every tool I could, and push to bring automation into the shop early, rather than wait. I'd also stay in my degree, since pharmacists with real judgement will still be needed for longer than software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd probably be working too much and sleeping too little, but I'd also feel the adrenaline. It's like being on the starting line of a race you didn't pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years: what's the first night like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's get ahead of it. If the machine counts the pills, then my job is to be the face that tells an anxious customer it will be all right. I'd put the shop's trust and personal service at the front of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could survive if we change fast enough, and if rules keep chain pharmacies from swallowing everything. If not, we might have to sell, and that would be hard for my mum. I'd hate that, and I'd work to avoid it.

say: I'd say we need **rules** so small shops aren't wiped out before adapting.
I'd offer to speak on a **student panel** about family pharmacies.
think: Privately I'd be **anxious and angry**: two years is too short to change a shop.
If a chain automates first, we could be **finished** before I qualify.
do: Sit down with my parents and go through the shop's **accounts**.
Learn every **tool** I can and push to automate the shop early.
feel: **Anxious**, with adrenaline, like a race I didn't pick.
S2.quote: If the machine counts the pills, then my job is to be the face that tells an anxious customer it will be all right.
fieldNote: Her response is **action first**: accounts, tools and early automation.
She sees **trust and personal service** as her family's edge.
She openly names **selling the shop** as the fear underneath.

steps.text: Sit down with my parents and go through the shop's accounts
Learn every pharmacy and AI tool I can
Push to bring simple automation into the shop early
Speak at the pharmacy association's student panel about small shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to adapt if small businesses can get help to buy the tools. I'd say we should let the market sort it out but keep it fair. I'd tell my mum we should start now, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be uneasy, but with a plan. Five years gets me qualified and in the shop, with a couple of years of running things before robots reach hands-on work. I'd feel I had a chance to make the shop stronger than it is now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take the clinical services courses, and slowly bring automation into the shop, starting with stock and ordering. I'd put savings aside, since I'll need to buy into the business at some point. I'd keep singing in the choir, since it keeps me human and keeps me calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. I like having a project, and the shop is a good one. I'd probably over-plan, but I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what do you do that you couldn't in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time to build a base: pharmacy skills, shop experience, a bit of business knowledge. If the shop works out, I take it over, and if it doesn't, I'll have skills that move into a hospital or a bigger firm, so I'm not standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you decide between the shop and a job somewhere else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decide by looking at the numbers, and at my mum's health, honestly. If the shop is solid, I'll stay. If not, I'll take a good hospital job and help from the side.

say: I'd say there's **time to adapt** if small businesses can buy the tools.
I'd say let the **market** sort it out, but keep it fair.
think: Privately I'm **uneasy, with a plan**: I'd run things for a couple of years first.
I'd have a chance to make the shop **stronger** than now.
do: Finish my degree, take **clinical services** courses, and bring in stock and ordering automation.
Put **savings** aside to buy into the business.
S3.quote: If the shop works out, I take it over, and if it doesn't, I'll have skills that move into a hospital or a bigger firm, so I'm not standing still.
fieldNote: She treats the shop as a **project**, which keeps her busy and steady.
Her **fallback** is a hospital or bigger firm, a practical hedge.
She thinks about **her mum's health** in the decision, a family detail.

steps.text: Take clinical services courses alongside my pharmacy degree
Bring automation into the shop slowly, starting with stock and ordering
Save money to buy into the family business later
Decide about taking over the shop by looking at the numbers and my mum's health

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, if we use it to build things people want. I'd say we should back small businesses and let the market do its work. I'd probably give a talk in a local business group about adapting early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm pretty calm. By then I'd be 29, running or co-running the shop, and the tools would be mature. I'd feel I had time to do it properly, and maybe even expand to a second branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take over more of the shop, and bring in automation in stages, each one paid for by the last. I'd keep learning every new tool, since I enjoy it. I'd also save for a flat, and invest a bit in a fund, because I like seeing money grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and positive. It feels like having a long road with good weather. I'd sing in the choir and probably annoy people with my enthusiasm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years: is there any risk you get complacent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes, because ten years can feel like forever until it isn't. I'd set myself yearly goals for the shop so I don't slide. A date on the calendar keeps me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it goes badly for small businesses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I blame big firms that use size to crush smaller ones, and governments that keep changing the rules. Small businesses that wait too long to adapt also have to take some responsibility, not only big firms that use size to crush smaller ones.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty if we build things people want.
I'd say we should back **small businesses** and let the market work.
think: Privately I'm **calm**: by 29 I'd be running the shop with mature tools.
I might even expand to a **second branch**.
do: Take over more of the shop and bring in **automation** in stages, each paid for by the last.
Save for a flat and put a little into a **fund**.
feel: **Calm and positive**, like a long road with good weather.
S4.quote: Small businesses that wait too long to adapt also have to take some responsibility, not only big firms that use size to crush smaller ones.
fieldNote: She **shares blame** with small businesses that wait, a self-critical move.
She plans **yearly goals** to avoid complacency.

steps.text: Take over more of the shop and add automation in stages
Put part of my earnings into an index fund
Save for a flat near the shop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my family's pharmacy is how we live, and two years isn't enough to change it or protect it. What would help is fair rules, so small businesses can afford the same tools as the big chains, and a clear idea of what pharmacists will be allowed to do. I'd rather have a fair market than a grant.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not afraid of the technology, but I'm careful about who owns it. I use it every day, and I want to be the one using these tools, not the one they replace. And I think people who help others should keep their hands on the controls.

headlineQuote: I want to be the one using these tools, not the one they replace.
portrait: Iris is 19, studying **pharmacy** with top results, a strong cushion and a family pharmacy to inherit.
She is traditional and adaptive: she uses AI **every day** and picks up new tools early.
She believes in **free markets**, hard work and family, and wants small firms to get the same tools.
Her mood is uneasy even in a plateau because of **chain pharmacies**, and anxious at two years.
She sees herself as the **face** and judgement of a pharmacy, and leans on her mum and choir.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because the family pharmacy would not have time to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair rules** so small businesses can afford the same tools as the big chains.
A clear idea of what **pharmacists** will be allowed to do.
